claim: The real numbers form a complete ordered field — every Cauchy sequence converges and the Dedekind completeness axiom holds

evidence.title: Continuity and Infinitesimals (SEP)
evidence.finding: Dedekind's 1872 construction provides a rigorous foundation for real numbers via cuts, establishing completeness

evidence.title: Real Numbers (SEP)
evidence.finding: The real number system is uniquely characterized (up to isomorphism) by the complete ordered field axioms

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Axioms are stipulated definitions, not empirical claims — completeness is a property of the construction
scoreReasoning.coherence: The reals are the unique complete ordered field; this is a mathematical theorem, not conjecture
scoreReasoning.convergence: Universal acceptance in standard analysis; constructivists accept a weaker version
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: All of physics, engineering, and applied mathematics uses real numbers as the number system

claim: The epsilon-delta definition of limits provides a rigorous foundation for continuity, convergence, and all of calculus

evidence.title: Continuity and Infinitesimals (SEP)
evidence.finding: Weierstrass's epsilon-delta formulation (1860s) finally made calculus rigorous after 200 years of informal use of infinitesimals

evidence.title: Analysis I (Tao 2006)
evidence.finding: Modern analysis textbooks build all of calculus on the epsilon-delta limit, demonstrating its sufficiency as a foundation

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Limits are a mathematical definition, not an empirical claim — their 'correctness' is about internal consistency
scoreReasoning.coherence: Epsilon-delta makes calculus fully rigorous; resolves all paradoxes of the infinitesimal
scoreReasoning.convergence: Standard foundation since the 19th century; nonstandard analysis offers an alternative but proves the same theorems
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Every application of calculus in science and engineering ultimately rests on limits

claim: The derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function — defined as the limit of the difference quotient, it captures velocity, slope, and sensitivity

evidence.title: Continuity and Infinitesimals — Derivatives (SEP)
evidence.finding: The derivative, rigorously defined as a limit, captures Newton's fluxions and Leibniz's infinitesimal ratios in a single precise framework

evidence.title: Calculus (Spivak)
evidence.finding: Spivak develops derivatives from first principles, proving the chain rule, product rule, and mean value theorem from the limit definition

scoreReasoning.correspondence: The derivative is a mathematical definition — its power lies in exactly capturing physical rates of change
scoreReasoning.coherence: Follows rigorously from limits; all rules (chain, product, quotient) are provable theorems
scoreReasoning.convergence: Universal acceptance in mathematics; the concept is unique and well-defined
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Velocity, acceleration, marginal cost, reaction rates — derivatives are everywhere in science and economics

claim: The Riemann integral measures the accumulated quantity under a curve — defined as the limit of Riemann sums, it captures area, work, and total change

evidence.title: Continuity and Infinitesimals — Integration (SEP)
evidence.finding: Riemann's definition of the integral (1854) as a limit of sums made integration rigorous; Lebesgue later generalized it

evidence.title: Calculus — Integration (Spivak)
evidence.finding: The Riemann integral is constructively defined and its properties (linearity, monotonicity, additivity) are provable theorems

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Integration is a mathematical construction — not empirically testable but exactly captures accumulation
scoreReasoning.coherence: Rigorously defined from limits; all properties are theorems, not assumptions
scoreReasoning.convergence: Universal acceptance; Lebesgue integration generalizes Riemann but doesn't replace it for continuous functions
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Area, volume, work, probability, signal processing — integration is ubiquitous in science

claim: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus establishes that differentiation and integration are inverse operations — the integral of a derivative recovers the original function (up to a constant)

evidence.title: Continuity — Fundamental Theorem (SEP)
evidence.finding: The FTC, proved rigorously by Cauchy and refined by Riemann, is one of the most important theorems in mathematics

evidence.title: Calculus — FTC Proof (Spivak)
evidence.finding: The theorem follows from the mean value theorem and the definition of the integral; the proof is constructive and elementary

scoreReasoning.correspondence: This is a proven mathematical theorem — its truth is established by proof, not experiment
scoreReasoning.coherence: Unifies the two central operations of calculus; considered one of the most beautiful results in mathematics
scoreReasoning.convergence: Universal acceptance; no challenge to the theorem has ever been raised
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Every practical computation of integrals (and most of physics) depends on the FTC

claim: Calculus provides rigorous, proven methods for analyzing continuous change, foundational to all quantitative science

evidence.title: Continuity and Infinitesimals (SEP)
evidence.finding: Calculus, made rigorous in the 19th century, remains the indispensable mathematical language of physics and engineering

evidence.title: Calculus (Spivak)
evidence.finding: The logical structure of calculus — from reals to limits to derivatives/integrals to FTC — is complete and self-contained

scoreReasoning.correspondence: Calculus as a system is not empirically testable — but its applications produce empirically verified predictions
scoreReasoning.coherence: Complete, self-contained mathematical framework built from axioms through proven theorems
scoreReasoning.convergence: Universal acceptance as the foundation of quantitative science; no competing framework for continuous analysis
scoreReasoning.pragmatism: Physics, engineering, economics, biology, computer science — virtually all quantitative fields depend on calculus
